rows.themeProjectDescription:
Project Background

Federated learning enables collaborative model training without raw data sharing, but local model updates still leak private information. Fixed differential privacy mechanisms fail to adapt to diverse client data distributions, leading to either excessive noise (low accuracy) or insufficient protection (privacy leakage). Adaptive differential privacy dynamically adjusts noise intensity according to data sensitivity and client characteristics, achieving better trade-off between privacy and utility. This project focuses on designing an adaptive differentially private federated learning framework to improve model performance under strong privacy guarantees.

Main Tasks

  1. Study the privacy leakage risks in federated learning and the principle of differential privacy.
  2. Analyze the influence of fixed noise on model accuracy in non-IID data scenarios.
  3. Design an adaptive differential privacy mechanism for federated learning.
  4. Implement a complete privacy-preserving federated learning system.
  5. Conduct experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and other datasets to evaluate accuracy, convergence speed and privacy protection level.
  6. Complete a standardized graduation thesis.

Expected Outcomes

System

  • A privacy-preserving federated learning prototype system based on adaptive differential privacy
  • Modules: adaptive noise generation, local training, secure aggregation, privacy budget management
  • Test scripts and visualization tools for accuracy, loss and privacy budget consumption
  • Comparison results with traditional federated learning methods

Graduation Thesis

  • Standard undergraduate thesis with complete structure
  • Literature review, system design, algorithm derivation, experimental analysis and conclusion
  • Charts of model accuracy, convergence speed and privacy-performance trade-off
  • Security and privacy analysis of the proposed method

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

In high-speed Serializer/Deserializer (SerDes) communication systems, signal integrity and link reliability are paramount. Bit Error Rate (BER) is the most critical metric for evaluating link quality. Due to the high cost of external bit error rate testers, embedding a BERT logic within the physical coding sublayer is a standard industry practice. Pseudo-Random Binary Sequences (PRBS) are widely used for this purpose because their spectral characteristics closely mimic true random data while remaining entirely deterministic and repeatable. Designing a pure RTL-based PRBS test system allows for on-chip link validation, which is essential for link training, system debugging, and channel performance evaluation.


2. Main Task


(1) Research the mathematical principles of PRBS generation, focusing on the characteristic polynomials and LFSR architectures for standard PRBS-7, PRBS-15, and PRBS-31 patterns.

(2) Design a dynamically configurable, multi-mode PRBS generator supporting seamless switching between PRBS-7, 15, and 31 modes via register control.

(3) Develop a PRBS synchronization detector that utilizes sliding bit-by-bit comparison and seed-loading mechanisms to automatically achieve phase alignment with the incoming data stream, ultimately outputting a stable sync-lock indicator.

(4) Design a robust bit-error comparison and statistical module capable of performing bit-level error counting, block error counting, and cumulative BER calculations, incorporating wide-bit counters to support extended operational periods without overflow.

(5) Develop a highly automated testbench capable of simulating both error-free and noise-injected channel environments. The testbench must execute automated simulations for no less than 1,000,000 bit cycles to thoroughly verify the synchronization capture mechanism and the accuracy of the error statistical module.


3. Expected Outcomes

A fully synthesizable Verilog RTL codebase encompassing the multi-mode PRBS generator, the synchronization detector, and the comprehensive error statistics module.

A detailed simulation verification report presenting synchronization capture timing diagrams and statistical accuracy metrics under various injected bit error rates.

A comprehensive graduation thesis detailing the mathematical foundations of LFSRs, the synchronization algorithm architecture, simulation waveform analyses, and a comprehensive evaluation of the system's BER detection capabilities.
rows.themeTitle: RTL Design of a Multi-Mode PRBS Bit Error Rate Test (BERT) System for High-Speed SerDes Links

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

In high-speed Serializer/Deserializer (SerDes) systems, the receiver must accurately extract the embedded clock and synchronize with the incoming data stream to ensure error-free transmission. Traditional analog Clock and Data Recovery (CDR) circuits are highly sensitive to Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) variations and face scaling challenges in advanced technology nodes. Consequently, All-Digital CDR (ADCDR) architectures have become mainstream. Among them, oversampling-based ADCDRs operate by sampling the incoming serial data multiple times per bit period to determine the optimal sampling phase digitally. This project focuses on the RTL design and verification of a 3x oversampling ADCDR, simulating a completely digital phase-tracking loop to achieve high-speed data recovery and jitter tolerance.


2. Main Tasks

Research the fundamentals of CDR in high-speed serial links, analyzing the pros and cons of mainstream architectures (e.g., oversampling vs. phase-interpolation), and thoroughly understand the phase detection mechanism of 3x oversampling.

Design the 3x oversampling module to sample the incoming serial data stream three times per bit period, generating Early, On-time, and Late decision signals.

Implement a Bang-Bang Phase Detector (BBPD) that utilizes the oversampled results to determine the relative position of the current sampling phase against data transitions, outputting explicit Lead or Lag phase-error indications.

Develop a Digital Loop Filter (DLF) and a Numerically Controlled Oscillator (NCO) to establish a closed-loop control system for phase tracking. The system should support a two-stage operational mode: coarse frequency locking followed by fine phase locking.

Develop a comprehensive testbench featuring a serial data source with programmable phase offsets and injected jitter. Perform automated simulations for no less than 10,000 bit periods to verify the CDR locking process, tracking performance, and recovery accuracy. Analyze lock time and jitter tolerance across different loop bandwidth configurations.


3. Expected Outcomes

A complete, synthesizable Verilog RTL codebase for the all-digital CDR, encompassing the oversampling data path, BBPD, DLF, and NCO modules.

A comprehensive simulation verification report detailing locking process waveforms, dynamic phase tracking curves, and performance comparisons under various loop parameter setups.

A graduation thesis documenting the CDR theoretical analysis, loop parameter derivations, simulation results, and jitter tolerance evaluations.
rows.themeTitle: RTL Design of an All-Digital Clock and Data Recovery (CDR) Circuit Based on 3x Oversampling

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

In advanced high-speed SAR ADCs, particularly those utilizing redundant or sub-radix-2 architectures, capacitor mismatch inevitably degrades dynamic performance parameters such as ENOB and SFDR. Foreground digital calibration is highly effective for addressing this: the exact capacitor weights are mathematically estimated offline (training phase) and then utilized to digitally reconstruct the raw analog samples in real-time (inference phase). While the weight estimation can be handled by open-source software like the ADCToolbox, the real-time inference demands a dedicated on-chip digital backend. This project focuses on designing the pure RTL hardware accelerator necessary to execute this weight reconstruction continuously at high clock frequencies without disrupting the data stream.


2. Main Task

The core objective is to design and verify a high-throughput digital backend for a 12-bit sub-radix-2 SAR ADC. The quantified tasks include:

(1) Research the error mechanics of capacitor mismatch in redundant SAR ADCs and utilize the open-source Python ADCToolbox to process sample datasets, extracting the optimal calibrated digital weights.

(2) Design the RTL architecture for the real-time weight reconstruction module. This involves mapping the extracted weights into internal registers and constructing a fully pipelined Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) tree capable of calculating the sum of products (W_i * B_i) in real-time.

(3) Optimize the Verilog codebase to achieve high-frequency timing closure. For instance, design a 4-to-5 stage pipeline architecture to ensure the logic path can meet aggressive timing constraints (e.g., targeting a 1 GHz clock domain for an ASIC implementation, or maximizing the Fmax on an FPGA target).

(4) Develop an automated testbench that streams raw, uncalibrated binary data from the Python toolkit into the Verilog simulation environment, captures the reconstructed output, and feeds it back to the ADCToolbox to verify that the calibrated ENOB matches the software-only ideal results.

(5) Synthesize and implement the RTL design on an FPGA development board, demonstrating real-time data processing and valid resource utilization (Logic Elements/DSP blocks).


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include:

- A fully synthesizable, deeply pipelined Verilog RTL codebase for the ADC digital reconstruction backend.

- A co-simulation framework bridging the Python ADCToolbox and the hardware Testbench, complete with spectral analysis graphs verifying ENOB and SFDR recovery.

- A comprehensive graduation thesis detailing the weight calibration theory, the RTL pipeline architecture, timing optimization strategies, and FPGA implementation results.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Modern 10 Gigabit Ethernet (10GbE) utilizes IEEE 802.3 64b/66b line coding to achieve 96.97% transmission efficiency. Because 66 is not a power of two, a "Gearbox" module is required to handle non-integer bit-width conversions between the 66-bit line rate and 64-bit internal buses. This project focuses on the RTL design and verification of the 10GBASE-R Physical Coding Sublayer (PCS).


2. Main Tasks

The project implements four core modules:

- Encoder/Decoder: Design 64b/66b parsing logic for both data and control frames.

- Parallel Scrambler: Develop a Python script to automatically derive and generate Verilog RTL for a 64-bit parallel scrambler/descrambler using the polynomial G(x) = x^58 + x^39 + 1.

- Block Lock FSM: Design a state machine (HUNT, CHECK, LOCK) to manage sync header tracking and alignment.

- Gearbox: Implement TX (64-to-66) and RX (66-to-64) modules using wide buffer registers and phase accumulators.


3. Expected Outcomes

Deliverables include synthesizable Verilog RTL, the Python code-generation script, and a comprehensive testbench. System stability will be validated through closed-loop simulations, demonstrating zero bit errors across 10,000+ clock cycles under various traffic scenarios. A complete graduation thesis documenting the design architecture and waveform analysis will also be produced.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1.Background


With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence technologies, techniques such as Text-to-Speech (TTS), Voice Conversion (VC), and voice cloning have become increasingly mature. Highly realistic "speech deepfake" samples (including synthetic speech, voice-converted speech, segmented/manipulated forgeries, etc.) are spreading rapidly across social media, remote identity verification, financial customer service, and meeting scenarios, posing significant risks of identity theft and fraud. Traditional detection methods based on handcrafted features and statistical models have limited generalization capabilities. When facing new, unknown forgery algorithms, it is difficult to meet practical defense requirements. Deep learning, with its powerful ability for automatic feature learning and end-to-end modeling, provides an effective approach to capture subtle traces within forged speech. Therefore, the research on speech deepfake detection methods based on deep learning holds significant theoretical importance and urgent practical value for establishing an active and precise defense system against forgery.


2. Main task


(1)   Analyze common spoofing/deepfake generation methods, typical artifacts, and the basic principles of detection (time–frequency artifacts, phase inconsistency,

spectral envelope anomalies, etc.);

(2)   Collect and organize public anti-spoofing datasets (e.g., ASVspoof 2019/2021 or other public subsets), and conduct preprocessing and feature construction (log-mel/LFCC) with data

augmentation such as noise, reverberation, and codec compression;

(3)   Design and implement a deep learning based speech deepfake detection model: start from a baseline (lightweight CNN/LCNN or AASIST) and improve generalization to unseen attacks

via attention or multi-scale time–frequency feature learning;

(4)   Develop training strategies and loss functions (cross-entropy/focal loss, imbalance handling), and conduct comparative and ablation studies with interpretability analysis

(Grad-CAM/attention maps) to evaluate robustness under different attack and channel conditions.

Technical Indicators:

1.Background

The biological retina is a high-performance front-end visual processing system that can perform complex visual operations such as light adaptation, motion detection and direction selectivity under low power consumption. Direction selectivity refers to the selective response of ganglion cells to motion stimuli in specific directions, which acts as the core physiological mechanism for biological motion perception and visual analysis. Traditional image sensors separate the photosensitive unit from the signal processing unit, resulting in high power consumption, large signal delay and poor real-time performance. Such limitations hinder their application in low-power wearable devices and bionic robots. To solve this problem, this project intends to construct a bionic retinal direction-selective visual circuit to reconstruct the multi-layer neural pathway of the retina. In this research, organic photodetectors are used to simulate biological photoreceptors for photoelectric conversion. Analog circuits are designed to replicate the signal regulation and transmission characteristics of bipolar cells, starburst amacrine cells and direction-selective ganglion cells. This study realizes the native direction-selective function of the retina at the hardware level, providing a feasible design scheme for low-power bionic visual hardware.

According to the multi-layer neural structure of the retina, the physiological functions of photoreceptors, bipolar cells, starburst amacrine cells and ganglion cells are mapped into corresponding circuit modules to establish the overall system framework.

(2) Design and construct analog circuit units to simulate the signal transmission characteristics of bipolar cells and the lateral inhibition mechanism of amacrine cells. The motion filtering characteristics of ganglion cells are realized through circuit logic to complete the core direction-selective function and relevant simulation verification.

(3) Complete PCB design, fabrication and welding to build a hardware test platform. Moving optical stimuli in different directions are applied to test the circuit and verify the directional response performance of the system.

(4) Test key performance parameters including response speed, direction selectivity index and static power consumption. Combined with biological visual mechanisms, the circuit characteristics are analyzed to realize iterative optimization and debugging.

3.Expected Outcomes

(1) Establish a complete design scheme for the bionic retinal direction-selective circuit, complete circuit simulation of each functional module, and retain systematic simulation data and analysis results.

(2) Construct a hardware prototype integrating photodetectors and analog neural circuits, which realizes the selective response to moving optical stimuli in specific directions at the physical hardware level.

(3) Collect and organize measured system data, quantitatively analyze key indicators including direction selectivity index, response speed and power consumption, and evaluate the comprehensive performance of the bionic circuit.

(4) Compile a graduation thesis summarizing system design, circuit simulation, hardware construction and experimental tests. This work verifies the feasibility of replicating retinal neural visual functions through analog circuits and provides references for the design of similar bionic visual circuits.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background

Understanding what a model does not know is a critical part of many machine learning systems. Today, deep learning algorithms are able to learn powerful representations that can map high dimensional data to an array of outputs. However, these mappings are often taken blindly and assumed to be accurate, which is not always the case and may cause disastrous consequences. In May 2016, there was the first fatality from an assisted driving system, caused by the perception system over-confidently confusing the white side of a trailer for bright sky [1]. Quantifying uncertainty in computer vision applications can be largely divided into regression settings such as depth regression, and classification settings such as semantic segmentation. Two inherently different sources of uncertainty, often referred to as aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, can be distinguished [2]. Aleatoric (aka statistical) uncertainty refers to the notion of randomness, that is, the variability in the outcome of an experiment which is due to inherently random

effects, and hence cannot be reduced. As opposed to this, epistemic (aka systematic) uncertainty refers to uncertainty caused by a lack of knowledge of data, and can in principle be reduced with additional information. As such, separately estimating (disentangling) these two types of uncertainties is of great importance. A very recent study benchmarked uncertainty disentanglement methods in the classification setting [3]. However, research in disentangling aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties in the regression setting is still quite limited. In this project, we will focus on estimating (disentangling) these two types of uncertainties for deep learning regression problems.


References

[1] A. Kendall and Y. Gal, "What Uncertainties Do We Need in Bayesian Deep Learning for Computer Vision?," in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), vol. 30, pp. 5574-5584, 2017.

[2] E. Hüllermeier and W. Waegeman, "Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning: an introduction to concepts and methods," Machine Learning, vol. 110, no. 3, pp. 457-506, 2021.

[3] B. Mucsányi, M. Kirchhof, and S. J. Oh, "Benchmarking Uncertainty Disentanglement: Specialized Uncertainties for Specialized Tasks," in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), vol. 37, 2024.


Main tasks

1) Literature reading. The student will read references recommended by the supervisor on uncertain estimation and disentanglement for deep learning regression models.

2) Method re-implementation. The student will re-implement the methods reported in the references by downloading the accompanying code and data and running them.

3) Comparison. The student will perform a systematic comparison across state-of-the-art methods to identify the comparative pros and cons of each approach.

4) Contribution. Upon completing all the aforementioned tasks, the student is expected to either refine existing approaches or adapt an established uncertainty disentanglement method to address a specific regression task, such as object detection.


Expected outcomes

A high-quality final-year project report that delivers an in-depth analysis of uncertainty disentanglement for regression problems, and ideally, incorporates novel refinements to existing approaches.
rows.themeTitle: Uncertainty disentanglement for deep learning regression

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1、Background

Humanoid robots are increasingly deployed in complex environments requiring agile, precise, and compliant movements—such as service robotics, healthcare assistance, and industrial collaboration. The joint actuation system directly determines a humanoid robot's dynamic performance, energy efficiency, and safety. Permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs) have become the dominant choice for joint drives due to their high torque density, fast dynamic response, and low rotor losses. However, achieving smooth, high-precision servo control under varying loads, limited joint space, and real-time constraints remains challenging. Classical PID control often fails to handle nonlinearities, parameter uncertainties, and external disturbances common in legged or bimanual manipulation tasks. Therefore, developing advanced yet practical servo control methods for PMSM-based humanoid robot joints is both academically meaningful and critical for real-world robot autonomy.

2、Project Content

This project focuses on designing, analyzing, and validating improved servo control strategies for a PMSM-driven robot joint. First, a mathematical model of the PMSM in the

dq-rotating reference frame is established, including electromagnetic torque and mechanical load dynamics. Then, a cascaded field‑oriented control (FOC) architecture is adopted as the baseline. To enhance tracking precision and disturbance rejection, two candidate methods are investigated: (1) a sliding mode controller (SMC) with a continuous approach law to reduce chattering while maintaining robustness, and (2) a model‑based active disturbance rejection controller (ADRC) that estimates and compensates lumped disturbances in real time. All controllers are first designed and tuned in MATLAB/Simulink, incorporating practical constraints such as current limits and PWM update delays. A hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation using a commercial robot joint module is planned for validation. Key performance metrics include step response overshoot, settling time, torque ripple, and trajectory tracking accuracy under dynamic loads. The final deliverable includes a comparative analysis of the proposed methods and a guideline for implementing the superior solution on embedded motor controllers for humanoid robots.

3、Expected Outcomes

1）A complete simulation model of the ANPC-based ESS grid-connected converter with MPC in MATLAB/Simulink.

2）Demonstration that MPC achieves faster dynamic response and lower current THD (e.g., <3%) than conventional PI control.

3）Analysis of neutral-point voltage balancing performance.

4） final project report documenting the design, simulation results, and practical implementation considerations.

The first part of the work is to define the target hardware and firmware, such as GRBL or Marlin, and design a reliable data collection subsystem for real or simulated G-code execution. The subsystem should record run summaries, periodic telemetry samples, machine states, positions, feedrate, and abnormal events during each drawing job.


The second part is to turn the collected telemetry into a usable prediction dataset. Planned features should be extracted from G-code and MotionTimeline, including planned time, draw/rapid distance, segment count, short segment count, corner count, pen up/down count, and feedrate statistics. The dataset should also include actual execution time, prediction error, and quality flags for abnormal runs.


The final part is to implement and compare time prediction methods. The baseline should use the deterministic planner result from MotionTimeline. The student should then implement a simple calibration method, at least one traditional regression model, and one neural-network residual model such as an MLP. The model should be evaluated using MAE, RMSE, and MAPE. A lightweight online ETA correction method should also be demonstrated using current elapsed time and execution progress.


Expected deliverables include a hardware/firmware profile, telemetry data export, cleaned training dataset, baseline and model comparison results, online ETA correction demo, and documentation explaining the data fields, model design, experiment setup, and limitations.
rows.themeTitle: Robotics Execution Telemetry and Time Prediction for G-code-based Drawing Systems

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1.Background


Laser drilling is a typical application in the field of laser processing, playing an irreplaceable role in precision manufacturing such as film cooling holes on aeroengine turbine blades and micro-holes on fuel injectors. Traditional laser drilling relies on the positioning mode of "scanning galvanometer + moving workbench", which suffers from multiple cumulative errors such as galvanometer drift, platform error, and calibration eviation. The position accuracy of micro-holes is difficult to meet the high-precision and high-efficiency processing requirements of high-end manufacturing.

The rotary dual prism, as a precision beam deflection device, achieves beam pointing control by rotating two prisms with the same wedge angle relative to each other. It possesses advantages such as high precision, no drift, and compact structure. However, the rapid and precise positioning of the dual prism relies on an efficient inverse solution algorithm, which determines the rotation angles of the two prisms from the target beam pointing. Traditional iterative algorithms are time-consuming and have poor convergence stability. The equivalent vector model proposed in recent years abstracts beam deflection as a vector synthesis

problem, enabling analytical calculation of the inverse solution and opening up a new path for high-speed and high-precision laser positioning.

This project aims to explore the fast positioning algorithm of dual optical wedges based on the equivalent vector model and its application in laser drilling, providing theoretical and technical support for enhancing the positioning performance of laser processing.

 

2. Main task


(1) Analyzing the beam deflection mechanism of the double optical wedge and establishing an equivalent vector model.


(2) Exploring a rapid inverse solution method based on the equivalent vector model and the minimum rotation path criterion.


(3) Design algorithms for accuracy verification and speed testing, and conduct simulation experiments.


(4) Setup a dual optical wedge experimental platform to compare, analyze, and verify the actual positioning accuracy and speed of the algorithm.


Technical Indicators:

(1)    Pointing angle error: less than 5 mrad


(2)    End-to-end positioning time: <0.2s

 

3.Expected outcomes


(1) A bachelor's thesis.


(2) A dual-wedge laser beam end-to-end positioning algorithm program;

rows.themeProjectDescription:
DeepFake detection has become an important research topic in multimedia security. Existing detection methods often rely on convolutional neural networks or vision transformers to extract facial features from individual frames. However, manipulation artifacts in DeepFake videos are not always isolated in a single local region. They may appear as correlated inconsistencies across multiple facial regions, such as the eyes, mouth, cheeks, skin texture, and facial boundaries. Hypergraph representation learning provides a flexible way to model such higher-order relationships, because one hyperedge can connect multiple related facial regions simultaneously.

This project aims to develop a DeepFake video detection framework based on hypergraph representation learning. First, face images or video frames will be cropped and encoded by a pre-trained convolutional neural network. The extracted feature map will then be divided into spatial tokens, where each token is treated as a node. Based on feature similarity or spatial proximity, K-nearest-neighbor hyperedges will be constructed to describe high-order relationships among facial regions. Finally, a hypergraph neural network or a simplified hypergraph propagation module will be implemented for real/fake classification.

The main challenges include how to construct meaningful facial-region hypergraphs, how to design an effective hypergraph-based detector, and how to evaluate the method on public DeepFake datasets or small-scale experimental subsets. The expected outcome is a Python-based prototype system, experimental results, and a graduation thesis.

rows.themeTitle: DeepFake Video Detection Based on Hypergraph Representation Learning

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Dense visual understanding in open-world scenarios is an important goal in computer vision. It requires segmentation systems to recognize an ever-growing set of categories over time while maintaining the ability to generalize to unseen classes. Continual open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (COVSS) addresses this need by combining vision-language models with sequential class learning, where a frozen semantic space such as CLIP serves as an external reference for class identity. This paradigm is essential for building practical systems capable of lifelong dense visual understanding.

 

This project aims to investigate how the semantic structure of the vision-language model influences continual learning behavior in open-vocabulary segmentation. There are two main challenges. The first is how to characterize the geometric relationships among class text embeddings in CLIP's semantic space, including inter-class distances, cluster structures, and topological neighborhoods. The second is how to establish quantitative connections between these semantic relationships and the per-class learning dynamics observed during sequential training, including positive transfer to semantically similar old classes, interference between semantically close classes, and forgetting patterns across tasks. Visualization tools, statistical correlation analysis, and controlled task-ordering experiments can be explored to uncover these connections.

 

The expected output should include a semantic visualization toolkit for segmentation class vocabularies, a per-class continual learning analysis framework that tracks individual class performance across sequential tasks, and empirical findings on whether and how CLIP's semantic structure can predict or explain continual learning outcomes such as forgetting and transfer. The analysis can be evaluated through correlation metrics, visual case studies, and comparison across different task orderings.

rows.themeTitle: Analysis of Vision-Language Semantic Dynamics for Continual Open-Vocabulary Segmentation

This project aims to explore how different tensor network structures can be optimally adapted to different data types. rows.themeProjectDescription: Hyperspectral images (HSIs) are massive 3D tensors capturing rich spatial and spectral information. However, their enormous data volume poses significant challenges for storage and transmission. While traditional tensor decomposition effectively compresses HSIs by exploiting their low-rank structures, standard decomposition algorithms are computationally expensive and memory-intensive. This project aims to design a fast, lightweight HSI compression and reconstruction pipeline using randomized and sketched tensor algorithms. By applying tensor sketching techniques, the heavy tensor decomposition process is significantly accelerated with a reduced memory footprint. The extracted low-rank factor matrices serve as the compressed representation of the HSI, which are subsequently multiplied to reconstruct the original image.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Low-light image enhancement is an important task in image processing and computer vision. It aims to improve the visibility of images captured under poor illumination while preserving details, colors, and natural appearance. Retinex theory provides an interpretable way to model low-light images by separating illumination and reflectance information. Such a model is useful for understanding and correcting the degradation caused by insufficient light.

 

This project aims to develop a Retinex-inspired low-light enhancement framework. There are two main challenges. The first is how to build a more effective degradation model for low-light images, considering illumination variation, noise, color distortion, and detail loss. The second is how to design a learning-based enhancement network that can combine the interpretability of Retinex modeling with the representation ability of deep neural networks. Optimization-inspired networks, attention mechanisms, or Transformer-based modules can be explored to improve the enhancement performance.

 

The expected system should be able to enhance low-light images automatically and produce visually pleasing results. The performance can be evaluated by both visual comparison and quantitative image quality metrics.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Media-Based modulation (MBM) was first proposed by Khandani as a new realization of index modulation (IM) for wireless communications, which embedded extra information by creating different channel states with the ON/OFF status of the radio frequency (RF) mirrors around each transmit antenna (TA). Recent studies have focused on the diversity design and detection algorithms for MBM systems. As the secrecy issue becomes significant in wireless networks, more and more researchers try to enhance the secrecy of MBM systems from the perspective of physical layer.

So far, most of the physical layer security (PLS) schemes are designed for time-division duplex (TDD) MBM systems with channel reciprocity. For example, Yildirim, Basar, and Kurt proposed a secure precoder, while Zhang and Zhao found the optimal input probability mass function maximizing the secrecy rate for single-input

multiple-output (SIMO) MBM systems when the channel state information (CSI) of the eavesdropping link is available. When the eavesdropping CSI is not available, different PLS schemes have been designed for TDD MBM systems in many other works. Although frequency-division duplex (FDD) has been widely used in practical wireless communication systems, very few studies have been done on the PLS problem in FDD MBM systems.

Zhou, Gao, and Liao proposed an AN-aided precoding scheme to enhance the security of FDD multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) MBM systems against eavesdropping, and the impact brought by feedback overhead was also analyzed. However, a closed-form solution was not derived in that work, which is often desirable because it can provide explicit analytical insights and reduce computational complexity in system design. Moreover, since abundant channel realizations can be generated in MIMO MBM systems, the feedback amount of MIMO MBM systems is obviously larger than that of conventional MIMO systems. The large amount of feedback in this study caused considerable overhead since all the legitimate channel fading realizations of the down link were fed back by the legitimate receiver.

The main tasks of this project include: (1) By reading relevant literature, become familiar with the basic principles of physical layer security and carefully study existing PLS schemes. (2) Construct a mathematical model of down-link and feedback transmission of FDD MIMO-MBM. (3) Learn the fundamentals of quantized feedback and consider possible ways to apply it to FDD MIMO-MBM systems to reduce feedback overhead. (4) Complete the formula derivation to obtain closed-form solution of the secrecy rate to characterize the secrecy performance of the scheme.

All numerical simulations in this project will be conducted using Matlab. Students who are proficient in Matlab programming and numerical modeling will be easy to finish this work. This research topic originates from cutting-edge advancements of wireless communication, it requires the recruited students spend sufficient energy and time. We welcome like-minded, driven individuals to join us. The students who expect to publish literatures after some practices in our group are sincerely welcome.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Electrooculography (EOG) is a technique that measures the corneo-retinal standing potential of the eye, allowing the detection of eye movements such as saccades, smooth pursuit, and blinks. Compared to video-based eye trackers, EOG is low‑cost, portable, and less affected by lighting conditions or head movements. It has been widely used in human‑computer interaction (HCI) for assistive technologies, hands‑free control, and virtual input systems. However, practical EOG‑based HCI systems must address challenges including signal noise, motion artifacts, real‑time processing, and wireless reliability. This project aims to design a complete wireless EOG acquisition and interaction system, from analog front‑end hardware to a PC‑based interactive application (e.g., a virtual keyboard), demonstrating the feasibility of EOG‑driven HCI with good usability and robustness.


2. Main Task

2.1 Study the characteristics of human EOG signals, investigate EOG acquisition techniques (hardware and software implementations), as well as sensor signal processing methods. Propose and refine the system design, perform component selection, and justify technical solutions.

2.2 Design an EOG acquisition system based on a mainstream analog front‑end (AFE) chip. Implement metal‑electrode‑based EOG signal acquisition and wireless data transmission.

2.3 Develop PC host software to visualise the EOG signal in real time. Design and implement an interactive application based on real‑time EOG signals, such as a virtual keyboard.


3. Expected Outcomes

A physical prototype capable of human EOG signal acquisition and wireless transmission. The prototype shall meet the following technical specifications:

3.1 Signal sampling rate and quality

Sampling rate: ≥ 250 Hz per channel (recommended 500 Hz)

Resolution: ≥ 16‑bit

Common‑mode rejection ratio (CMRR): ≥ 80 dB

Number of channels: ≥ 2.

3.2 Wireless transmission

Support Wi‑Fi (e.g., 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n)

Data rate: > 1 MB/s (sustained for real‑time streaming)

Packet loss rate: < 1%

3.3 Interactive design

Implement at least one EOG‑based interactive system (e.g., virtual keyboard)

Good demonstration value (e.g., intuitive visual feedback, low latency, robust to unintended blinks)

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Arterial auscultation is a critical non‑invasive technique for assessing cardiovascular health, including blood pressure measurement via Korotkoff sounds, detection of arterial bruits (which may indicate stenosis or aneurysm), and evaluation of peripheral blood flow. Traditional acoustic stethoscopes remain the primary tool for such tasks; however, they suffer from several intrinsic limitations: low sensitivity to low‑frequency arterial signals (typically 20–200 Hz), significant sound attenuation through hollow tubing, susceptibility to ambient noise, and reliance on the examiner’s auditory perception and experience. Moreover, conventional stethoscopes cannot record, store, or quantitatively analyze auscultation signals, hindering telemedicine applications and automated diagnosis.

Recent advances in micro‑electro‑mechanical systems (MEMS) have introduced silicon microphones that offer high sensitivity, flat frequency response down to sub‑Hz ranges, low power consumption, excellent phase consistency, and immunity to radio‑frequency interference. These characteristics make silicon microphones particularly suitable for capturing subtle arterial sound waves through the skin. By integrating a silicon microphone with embedded signal conditioning, wireless transmission, and intelligent software, a modern arterial auscultation system can overcome the drawbacks of traditional stethoscopes. It enables real‑time listening, high‑fidelity recording, remote monitoring, and advanced feature extraction (e.g., Mel‑spectrogram analysis) for objective vascular assessment. This project aims to design and implement such a system, providing a low‑cost, portable, and quantifiable solution for arterial auscultation that can serve both clinical and home‑care scenarios.


2. Main task

2.1 Investigate mainstream electronic stethoscope technologies and their hardware/software implementation methods, as well as arterial sound signal processing techniques. Propose and refine the system design, complete component selection, and conduct solution feasibility studies.

2.2 Design an arterial auscultation hardware system based on a silicon microphone sensor, enabling arterial sound signal acquisition, real‑time headphone playback, and wireless data transmission.

2.3 Design a PC host computer (upper‑computer) software to visualize auscultation signals and extract features.


3. Expected outcomes

Complete a physical prototype of the system that supports arterial sound signal acquisition, real‑time headphone playback, and wireless transmission, with the following technical specifications:

3.1 Sound sampling rate and audio quality:

Sampling rate: ≥ 22.05 kHz (or 44.1 kHz preferred) to adequately capture arterial sounds.

Resolution: 16‑bit ADC per channel.

Signal‑to‑noise ratio (SNR): ≥ 60 dB (A‑weighted).

3.2 Power consumption: Operating current < 20 mA; supports continuous operation for more than 6 hours.

3.3 Wireless transmission: Supports BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) with data rate > 200 kB/s and packet loss rate < 1%.

3.4 Data processing: Supports Mel‑spectrogram feature analysis.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Project Description:

Network coverage is a fundamental challenge in wireless sensor networks (WSNs), particularly in complex three-dimensional (3D) environments such as underwater monitoring systems. In Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks (UWSNs), reliable sensing performance depends heavily on effective sensor node placement to achieve high volumetric coverage while minimizing uncovered regions and excessive sensing overlap. Unlike conventional 2D deployment models, underwater applications require 3D modeling since sensors operate at different depths and must monitor volumetric regions. This project extends traditional 2D WSN coverage optimization into a 3D underwater deployment environment. The main objective is to model and optimize sensor node placement within a 3D underwater space to maximize volumetric coverage and improve deployment efficiency. The study focuses primarily on geometric coverage optimization rather than detailed underwater acoustic channel modeling. The optimization problem is computationally challenging due to the large search space associated with increasing sensor numbers and possible deployment locations. To address this challenge, the project investigates several well-known nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization techniques, including Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), and Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO). Each algorithm will be comparatively evaluated based on:

1. Volumetric coverage ratio

2. Computational efficiency

3. Solution robustness and stability across multiple simulation runs

Simulation models and 3D visualizations of underwater sensor deployment and coverage performance will be implemented using MATLAB.


Main Tasks:

1. Conduct a literature review on 3D underwater wireless sensor networks (UWSNs), coverage challenges, and nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization algorithms.

2. Develop a 3D simulation model to represent underwater sensor node deployment, incorporating coverage maximization.

3. Implement metaheuristic optimization algorithms (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Ant Colony Optimization, and Grey Wolf Optimizer) for optimal 3D node placement.

4. Visualize and analyze 3D sensor coverage using MATLAB.

5. Evaluate algorithm performance in terms of coverage rate, computational efficiency, solution robustness, and stability across multiple simulation runs.

6. Conduct a comparative analysis of metaheuristic algorithms to determine the most effective methods for 3D UWSN deployment optimization.

7. Document the simulation development process, algorithm implementation, experimental results, and practical insights for future deployment scenarios.

8. Troubleshoot technical issues systematically using critical thinking and problem-solving skills.


Expected Results/Objectives:

1. Develop a functional 3D simulation model for underwater sensor network deployment and volumetric coverage assessment.

2. Identify the most effective metaheuristic algorithms for optimizing 3D UWSN coverage under realistic constraints.

3. Produce visualizations and analyses demonstrating 3D sensor placement efficiency and coverage performance.

4. Enhance student skills in MATLAB simulation, optimization techniques, 3D data visualization, and collaborative problem-solving.

5. Deliver a comprehensive report summarizing methodology, algorithm comparisons, simulation results, and recommendations for practical 3D UWSN deployment.

Project Description:

Robot manipulators are widely used in industrial automation, smart manufacturing, and robotic applications where accurate trajectory control is essential. In practical systems, however, small variations in robot joint motions—caused by actuator noise, sensor inaccuracies, or external disturbances—can affect the final movement accuracy of the robotic arm. This project investigates how variations in joint angular velocities influence the trajectory performance of a planar 3-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) robotic manipulator. The main objective is to analyze and visualize the sensitivity of robot trajectories under different operating conditions and parameter variations. To improve computational efficiency, the project will explore data-driven surrogate modeling techniques that can approximate system behavior without requiring excessive repeated simulations. Methods such as Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW), Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation, and other lightweight surrogate modeling approaches will be investigated to accelerate trajectory analysis. Students will develop simulation models and perform comparative analysis to evaluate how surrogate-assisted methods can support faster and more efficient robotic trajectory studies. The project provides hands-on experience in robotic simulation, MATLAB programming, data-driven modeling, and engineering system analysis. The project is designed as a guided learning experience, and continuous support will be provided throughout the project duration.


Main Tasks:

1. Conduct a literature review on 3-DOF planar robot manipulators, trajectory optimization, and uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods.

2. Model the 3-DOF robot manipulator in MATLAB, including forward kinematics.

3. Simulate parametric uncertainty in joint angular velocities and evaluate its impact on end-effector trajectory accuracy.

4. Develop data-driven surrogate models (e.g., Radial Basis Functions) to approximate system responses efficiently.

5. Apply sampling-based uncertainty quantification techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo, Latin Hypercube Sampling) to assess trajectory robustness under realistic perturbations.

6. Visualize and analyze the impact of uncertainty on trajectories, comparing surrogate model predictions with full simulation results.

7. Document simulation models, surrogate modeling methods, experimental results, and analysis of robustness and trajectory deviations.

8. Troubleshoot technical issues systematically using critical thinking and problem-solving skills.


Expected Results/Objectives:

1. Develop a functional simulation model of a 3-DOF planar robot manipulator with joint-space uncertainty.

2. Apply surrogate-based modeling techniques to enable rapid evaluation of trajectory deviations due to parameter perturbations.

3. Quantify the robustness of optimal trajectories under realistic system uncertainties.

4. Generate visualizations demonstrating the impact of uncertainty and surrogate model accuracy on end-effector trajectories.

5. Enhance students’ skills in MATLAB simulation, surrogate modeling, uncertainty quantification, and collaborative problem-solving.

6. Deliver a comprehensive project report summarizing methodology, surrogate model performance, trajectory analysis, and recommendations for robust trajectory design.

Project Description:

Modern antenna design heavily relies on electromagnetic (EM) simulations to evaluate antenna performance characteristics such as reflection coefficient, bandwidth, and radiation patterns. Although full-wave EM simulations provide accurate results, they are often computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially when repeatedly used during antenna parameter optimization. This project investigates the use of data-driven surrogate modeling techniques to accelerate antenna design optimization while reducing computational cost. Surrogate-Based Optimization (SBO) is an intelligent optimization approach in which a fast mathematical approximation model—also known as a surrogate or metamodel—is used to replace expensive simulation evaluations during the optimization process. These surrogate models are closely related to Machine Learning (ML) supervised modeling techniques. The project focuses on optimizing antenna geometry parameters using data-driven surrogate modeling approaches such as Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) and Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation methods. Techniques such as Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) and grid search strategies will also be explored for efficient data generation and parameter exploration. Students will develop simulation and optimization models to evaluate how surrogate-assisted methods can improve antenna performance while significantly reducing optimization time and computational effort. Different surrogate weighting strategies and modeling approaches will be analyzed and compared in terms of prediction accuracy and optimization efficiency. This project provides students with hands-on experience in antenna simulation, optimization, AI-inspired modeling, and computational engineering techniques using MATLAB and related simulation tools. The advisor will provide continuous guidance and support throughout the project.


Main Tasks:

1. Conduct a literature review on antenna design optimization, surrogate modeling techniques, and data-driven optimization approaches.

2. Develop a simulation model using MATLAB Antenna Design Toolbox or CST to analyze antenna geometry parameters and performance characteristics.

3. Learn and apply data-driven surrogate modeling techniques, namely Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation beside Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) method for sampling design.

4. Optimize antenna geometry parameters using surrogate-based optimization to improve performance while reducing computational cost.

5. Evaluate optimized antenna designs, comparing surrogate-based optimization results with traditional methods like Genetic Algorithm (GA).

6. Visualize simulation results and optimized designs for clear performance assessment.

7. Document the development process, methodology, optimization procedures, experimental results, and analysis of findings.

8. Troubleshoot technical issues systematically using critical thinking and problem-solving skills.


Expected Results/Outcomes:

1. Develop a functional simulation model for antenna geometry analysis and performance evaluation.

2. Apply surrogate-based optimization to enhance antenna performance efficiently while reducing computational effort.

3. Identify the most effective surrogate modeling techniques for antenna design optimization.

4. Provide comparative insights between surrogate-based and traditional optimization methods.

5. Improve student skills in MATLAB simulation, surrogate modeling, optimization techniques, and collaborative problem-solving.

6. Deliver a comprehensive report detailing the methodology, optimization results, visualizations, and recommendations for future antenna design improvements.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
With the global demand for energy conservation, high power density, and system miniaturization, wide-bandgap (WBG) semiconductors have emerged as a foundational technology driving the revolution of power electronic systems, widely applied in electric vehicle (EV) fast charging, renewable energy systems, data center power supplies.Distinguished from traditional silicon-based semiconductors, WBG semiconductors possess superior material properties that enable them to operate stably at higher temperatures (up to around 300 °C) and support device designs with higher blocking voltage capability, addressing the performance bottlenecks of conventional semiconductor devices in harsh working environments and high-power applications.

In practical engineering applications, converter optimization is crucial to maximizing the performance advantages of WBG semiconductors, as switching losses constitute a significant portion of the overall system loss budget and directly determine the system’s efficiency, power density, and thermal management design. Targeting this core demand in power electronic system design, this project focuses on the development of universal analytical switching loss models for typical SiC-based half-bridge configurations, which are the basic building blocks of most power converter topologies. Specifically, two universal analytical switching loss models are separately proposed: one for the SiC MOSFET and Schottky diode half-bridge, and another for the SiC MOSFET half-bridge that incorporates temperature-dependent reverse recovery losses of body diodes. Both models are established based on data sheet information, including parasitic parameters that significantly affect switching performance in practical applications, ensuring high accuracy and strong applicability in engineering practice while maintaining computational efficiency. This project provides a reliable technical tool for the optimal design of WBG semiconductor-based power converters, facilitating the widespread application of WBG technologies in high-efficiency, high-power electronic systems.
